newsitem.title: COLOMBIA: Colombia's Samper sees broad anti-U.S. sentiment.
newsitem.headline: Colombia's Samper sees broad anti-U.S. sentiment.

text.p: Colombia, once a staunch supporter of the United States, has become the most anti-American country in Latin America, President Ernesto Samper was quoted on Monday as saying.

"Colombia was the most pro-American country in the region," Samper told the weekly news magazine Semana, referring to what he described as the status quo before U.S.-Colombia ties plunged into unprecedented crisis over his alleged ties to drug lords. "Now, negative sentiment has flourished among the people with respect to the United States. I'd say it's the most negative in the hemisphere."

Samper gave no specific example of anti-U.S. sentiment in Colombia -- a country where "but take me with you" is sometimes jokingly added to the anti-American war cry of "Yankee go home." But he has warned repeatedly that U.S. efforts to isolate Colombia and punish it economically because of its alleged failure to fight drug traffickers could backfire by fuelling widespread resentment.

Colombia is the world's largest supplier of cocaine and a leading supplier of heroin to the United States, the world's largest consumer of illicit drugs. Government officials argue that this should create a bond between the two countries -- and greater understanding in their joint anti-drug efforts -- rather than the mutual antagonisms and deep distrust that have marred their relationship since Samper's election in 1994.
Samper, whose U.S. travel visa was revoked in July, has been dogged by charges, which he denies, that he accepted millions of dollars in drug money to win his country's top job.

Semana, Colombia's most influential news weekly, named Samper "Man of the Year" in its latest issue that hit newsstands on Monday because of his ability to survive the political crisis stemming from those charges and from the open U.S. hostility to his government.
